opener.heading: Week 13: Easter & April Fools' Fun 🐰
about: Seven days of hiding things, finding them, and getting at the inside of something you cannot see into. Azlyn digs plastic eggs out of a bin of torn paper, builds a nest that dries overnight with five eggs waiting beside it, dyes eight eggs in fizzing paste, races them down a propped plank, hides twelve parcels and talks you in with hot and cold, sows cress that takes six mornings to show, and sorts four eggs into raw and cooked without cracking one. The same question comes at her in a new shape each day: what is in there, and how do you find out?

Easter Sunday lands on Day 87 and takes the whole day, from the paper trail off the doorstep to the chalked finish line. Good Friday opens the week with quiet roads and loud birds, and April Fools' Day closes it with three tricks she plans for Joseph and one hour of holding a secret. Two things outlast the week. The cress on the sill needs six days and a chart she colors one box a morning, and the paper bin set up on Friday stays out until somebody needs the tub back.
azlyn: Counting she cares about getting right. Twelve parcels hidden and twelve found, eight eggs down the ramp, five foil eggs into the nest, eight spoons of salt into the jar.
Guessing first, then finding out. She sorts a tray of objects into sink and float with no water in sight, commits to it, and tests every one.
Sorting by something she cannot see. Hatched or born, argued out over twenty cut-out animals, with the frog and the bat settled by a book.
Fiddly hand work. Tearing newspaper for an hour, packing wet paste round a shell, rolling foil eggs between her palms, pinching cress seed onto wet paper.
Waiting six days for a result. The cress goes in on Monday and pays out the following Sunday, and every morning in between she waters it and colors a box.
you: Sensory bins buy focus, and novelty is not the reason
Magical thinking peaks right about now, and it's healthy
Chemical reactions she can see are the best first science
Anticipation is a bigger pleasure than the payoff
Prediction is the beginning of scientific thinking
Category words are a bigger deal than they look
Lining things up is a developmental stage, not a red flag

An old bedsheet to lay underneath it
Newspaper, a big stack, and every piece of junk mail you have saved
Plastic eggs, 8–10 (scrunched foil balls or paper twists do the same job)
Kitchen foil, 1 roll
Paper cups, 6
A scoop, and a sieve or a small colander
Serving spoons, 2, and teaspoons, 4
A long spoon that reaches the bottom of a tall jar
A basket or a shallow box for Friday, before she builds her own on Saturday
Cereal boxes, 3, and an ice-cream tub for the basket
Thick card, 4 sheets (the headband, the basket handle, the word cards)
Masking tape, 2 rolls
Scissors
Crayons
Washable non-toxic poster paint
Permanent markers, 2
A pen, for writing her sentences down in her own words
A glue stick
Plain paper, a stack, including 4 sheets of letter paper for the book
Paper scraps and tissue
Paper plates, 3
Paper bags, 2
All-purpose flour, 500 g
Eggs, 18. Eight get dyed on Sunday, six get spun and cracked on Tuesday, and Monday wants six shell halves saved out of Sunday night's cooking
Baking soda, 1 box
White vinegar, 500 ml
Food coloring, 3–4 colors
Table salt, a full tub. Eight tablespoons go into one jar
A muffin tin, or 4 cups instead
Tall clear jars or glasses, 2
A clean jam jar with the label off
An egg carton
A cereal bowl, a large mixing bowl and 2 bowls for the sink-and-float sort
A grocery bag or plastic wrap to line the cereal bowl
A pitcher
A deep tray, and a shallow one for Kreston
Paper towels, 1 roll
Old towels, 2, and a dish towel
A freezer bag, and soap at the sink
Cress or mustard seed (bird seed or dried lentils work)
A dried bean
Carrots, a bag. One bowl chopped, one whole for the doorstep, one cooked soft for Kreston
Onions, 4, for the papery skins (the Around the World egg dye)
A saucer
A plank or a big flattened box for the ramp, and 2 heavy books to prop it
Chalk
String, a ball, with 2 lengths cut for the sorting circles
A tape measure
A flashlight with fresh batteries
A blanket for the tunnel
Tissue or a rolled sock for the rabbit tail
Twigs, moss and dry grass, gathered on Friday's walk
Magazines, a seed catalog or last year's calendar, anything with twenty animals in it
An animal book off the shelf, to settle the arguments
A lump of playdough, or scrunched paper instead
A laundry basket
Twelve small things worth finding (a hair clip, a sticker sheet, a wooden block, a teaspoon)
Eight things to sink or float (a cork, a stone, a plastic lid, an orange)
A clean burp cloth and 2 wooden spoons for Kreston
Your phone, charged, for the photo finish, the sill and the line down the hall
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 9 months this week. He hauls himself upright on anything that takes his weight, picks a paper strip off the floor with finger and thumb, and waves at every dog, goat and stranger you pass.

days.title: The Nest Bin
days.prepTonight: Set the big tub on the old bedsheet in the middle of the floor, bury the plastic eggs in the bottom, and stack the newspaper and junk mail beside it.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Nest You Can Dig In

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Counting Cars on a Quiet Morning

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Nest That Holds Five Eggs

opening.title: Tearing the Grass
opening.need: the newspaper stack · junk mail · the tub on its sheet.
steps: Sit her on the sheet beside the tub and show her how to tear one sheet of newspaper down its length.
Hand her the pile. She tears, you tear, and it all goes in the tub as it comes.
Fill it past her wrists. Tell her something is buried under there and leave it at that until 9:15.

main.title: The Nest You Can Dig In
materials: 1 large plastic storage tub or a deep cardboard box
A stack of newspaper and junk mail, torn
8–10 plastic eggs (scrunched foil balls or paper twists work)
1 basket for the eggs she finds
1 scrap of paper, 1 marker and masking tape for the total
steps: Basket beside her, hands only, no tools. She digs the eggs out one at a time.
Count them into the basket out loud. Write the total on a scrap and tape it to the tub.
Hand over the cups, the scoop, the spoon and the sieve.
Turn your back while she reburies them. Hunt when she says go, and miscount on purpose so she can put you right.
Bury a cup and a spoon in with the eggs before the next dig.
Leave the tub where it is. She comes back to it at 4:15 and it stays out all week.
main.tip: The sheet saves you. Gather the four corners and tip the lot back in, ten seconds instead of a vacuum.

outside.title: Counting Cars on a Quiet Morning
paras: Good Friday, so the roads are quiet. Stand at the corner and count the cars that pass in two minutes, then count again outside the stores. Write both numbers on the fridge to hold against a Tuesday. Fill her paper bag on the way back with twigs, moss and dead grass for 1:00.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and his pincer grip arrived this month, so a thumb and one finger take a strip of paper off the floor and into his mouth. Tape a sheet of foil flat to a piece of card for him instead and keep him an arm's length from the tub. In the stroller he waves at every dog you pass. Wave back and name them.

second.title: The Nest That Holds Five Eggs
second.intro: Good Friday, the quiet start of the Easter weekend, and the afternoon matches it. She packs a bowl with paste and torn paper, and it stands overnight before it is a nest.
materials: 1 grocery bag or plastic wrap to line it
All-purpose flour and water, mixed to a paste
Twigs, moss and dry grass from the walk
steps: Line the bowl with the grocery bag pressed into the curve, edges hanging over the rim. That is what lifts the nest out tomorrow.
Mix a cup of flour with enough water to make it like thick custard. She stirs.
She dips a strip, pulls it between two fingers to strip the extra off, and lays it in the bowl. Cross them over each other, three layers deep.
Press the twigs, moss and grass into the last layer while it is wet, ends poking out. A real nest is scruffy outside and smooth inside.
Roll five foil eggs between her palms, one at a time, and number them 1 to 5 with the marker.
Stand the bowl somewhere warm to dry, five hours or overnight, sit the eggs in a cup beside it, and let her count them in before bed.
second.tip: The paste goes cold and gluey and she may not want a hand in it. Hand her a fork to lift the strips and she stays at the table.

alternatives: Line the bowl and pack it with dry grass and twigs only, no paste.
Foil eggs alone, a bowlful of them, hidden back in the bin.
Make one enormous nest out of the bedsheet and sit in it.
outAgain: Playgroup, if it is running on Good Friday. Call ahead
A friend's house, with foil eggs to hide in their yard
The park, looking for nests in the tall trees at the edge
The yard, and shake the paper strips out there instead of indoors

aroundWorld.title: Easter Eggs Everywhere 🥚
paras: Painted eggs go far beyond Easter Sunday. Ukrainian pysanky are drawn in hot beeswax and dipped through a run of dyes, and one egg can take a day. Greek families dye eggs deep red on Holy Thursday and crack them point to point across the table. Whoever holds the last whole egg takes the year's luck. Persian families set painted eggs on the Nowruz table, one for each person in the house.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Boil eggs in water with the papery skins of four onions. They come out deep russet with no dye at all, and they are still eggs, so have them for lunch.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The pointed end of an egg is the strong end, which is why the Greek game starts point to point.

days.krestonPM: Kreston is 9 months and hauls himself upright on anything that takes his weight, a bowl of paste included. Set him on the floor with a clean bowl, a wooden spoon and a folded dish towel to haul out of the bowl. He bangs the spoon on the rim and checks your face to see whether the noise was allowed. Nod back.

insight.headline: Sensory bins buy focus, and novelty is not the reason.
paras: Azlyn will stay with that tub longer than she stays with most toys, and her hands are what hold her. Digging, pouring and sifting send a steady stream of information up from her fingertips, and that input organizes attention. Occupational therapists lean on it hard: a scattered child settles once her hands have something with texture and resistance to work through. The tub has no right answer in it, nothing to finish and nothing to get wrong, so the part of her that checks whether she is doing it right switches off. She gets a long stretch of thinking with no interruptions.

days.safety: The tub holds plastic eggs, foil balls and small twigs, all of them sized for Kreston's new pincer grip and all of them heading straight for his mouth. Keep him out of the tub and sweep the strips before he is on the floor. He pulls to stand on anything at his height, and a storage tub tips over onto a baby leaning on the rim. Push it against a wall or lift it onto the table between rounds.

days.title: Ears and a Tail
days.prepTonight: Flatten a cereal box onto the table with the masking tape, scissors and a rolled sock, and chop a bowl of carrot. Hard-boil eight eggs tonight for tomorrow and leave them in the fridge.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Basket with Her Name On

opening.title: Cutting the Ears
opening.need: last night's nest in its bowl · the five foil eggs · 1 flattened cereal box · 1 strip of paper or card · masking tape · scissors.
steps: Lift last night's nest out of the bowl by the bag edges, peel the bag off the inside, and let her count the five numbered eggs into it before anything else starts.
She draws two long ears on the flat box, and you leave the drawing alone and cut them out while she holds the box steady. She colors the insides whatever she picks.
Measure the paper strip round her head, tape it into a band, and tape the ears on. Say nothing more about rabbits until 9:15.

main.title: A Rabbit for the Day
materials: 1 strip of paper or card for a headband
Scrunched tissue or a rolled sock for the tail
2 dining chairs and 1 blanket for the tunnel
steps: Tape the tail to the back of her pants. Loop of tape, sticky side out, pressed flat. It falls off. Retape it.
Build the course together: cushions to hop across, the two chairs with the blanket over them as the tunnel, and the corner beyond the tunnel as the burrow.
Rabbits go with both feet at once. Show her, then let her run it.
Time her on the phone and read the number out. Run it again. She gets faster once she knows the route.
Change one thing each round: an extra cushion, the tunnel moved, the whole course backwards.
Bring the carrot bowl down off the table at the end, with Kreston up in the high chair, and eat them in the burrow. Rabbits eat sitting down.
main.tip: Put ears on yourself. A three-year-old drops a game the moment the adult looks embarrassed.

outside.title: Where a Rabbit Would Live
paras: Walk the hedges and the long grass at the edge of the park and hunt for the places a rabbit would pick: a gap under a fence, a hole at the foot of a bank, bramble with a tunnel worn through the bottom. Hop the last hundred yards home.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand on the sofa, the chairs and you. Lay the blanket tunnel low and set him at one end with a wooden spoon at the other, and leave the carrot bowl up on the table until he is in the high chair. He watches Azlyn hop and bounces on his knees to copy her. Give him a cooked carrot stick soft enough to squash between your fingers, and hold the other end of it.

second.title: The Basket with Her Name On
second.intro: Tomorrow morning she needs something to carry eggs in, so this afternoon she builds it.
materials: 1 strip of thick card for the handle
A handful of the torn paper from Friday
steps: Cut the tub down to the height of her hand, all the way round. Keep the offcuts.
Cut a handle from thick card, long enough to arch over with a hand's width underneath. Tape both ends inside, then tape over the joins twice more.
Hand it over. Crayons, paint, paper scraps stuck on, inside and out, and no steering from you.
Write her name across the front in marker while she watches, saying each letter as it goes down.
Line it with a handful of Friday's paper strips.
Load six things into it and let her carry it round the house by the handle. Mend what tears now rather than at seven tomorrow morning.

At bedtime she sets the carrot on a saucer out on the doorstep and leaves the basket beside it, and once she is asleep the carrot goes, the basket moves to a room at the far end of the house, and a paper trail runs from the doorstep to wherever you put it.
second.tip: Every homemade basket fails at the handle, and it fails while it is full.

alternatives: Decorate a shopping bag instead and call it a basket.
Build a second basket for Kreston, empty, for tipping out.
Draw the rabbit that comes for the carrot and leave the drawing beside it.
outAgain: The farm, and go straight to whatever has babies in it this week
The park with the ears still on
The garden center, for the bulbs coming up in the outdoor rows
The pet store, to watch how a real rabbit sits
days.krestonPM: Take him to the farm and hold him at the fence rather than putting him down. At 9 months he waves at the goats, the tractor and the woman selling tickets. Animals are loud close up, so watch his face and step back before he asks you to. At home, give him the basket offcuts one piece at a time and take back anything he tears small.

insight.headline: Magical thinking peaks right about now, and it's healthy.
paras: Azlyn puts a carrot on the step and half believes something will come for it. She holds two ideas at once: a rabbit that visits in the night, and the memory of you carrying the chocolate in from the car. Three-year-olds run that contradiction without distress, and researchers who study pretend find the frame stays under the child's control. She knows which one is true, and she picks the better story. The same machinery lets her be a doctor at the table and a dog under it, and rich pretend play tracks with stronger perspective-taking later on. Answer her questions and follow where she takes it.

days.safety: Chopped raw carrot is a choking hazard for a 9-month-old, and the burrow snack puts a bowl of it on the floor at his height. Kreston's carrot is cooked soft and held at one end by you, and Azlyn's bowl goes down only while he is up in the high chair or on your hip. Keep the blanket tunnel low and open at both ends, and never leave him inside it. The tape loops come off her tail all morning and land where he crawls, so pick each one up as it goes. Scissors go back out of reach the moment the ears are cut.

days.title: The Fizzing Eggs and the Egg Roll
days.prepTonight: The eggs are boiled, the trail is laid and the carrot is gone. Stand the vinegar, the baking soda and the coloring on the counter.

opening.title: Following the Trail
opening.need: the paper trail laid last night · the empty saucer · her basket.
steps: Send her to the doorstep first. The carrot is gone and the trail starts there.
Follow it at her pace. Let her carry every piece rather than tidying behind her.
The basket is at the end of it. Sit on the floor while she goes through it and do not rush her toward 9:15.

main.title: The Fizzing Egg Dye
materials: 500 ml white vinegar in a small pitcher
Paper towels and an old towel
steps: Half fill four cups of the muffin tin with baking soda. Two spoons of water and six drops of coloring into each, stirred to a thick paste. She does the drops and the counting.
Set the tray in front of her on the towel. Everything from here happens inside it.
She packs paste around an egg with her fingers until the shell has gone, then stands it in the tray. All eight, mixing colors on the last few.
Spoon vinegar over one egg. It foams up over her fingers, the paste slides off, and the color stays on the shell.
Let her do the other seven at her own speed. She will pour far too much. The tray takes it.
Rinse each one under the tap, pat it dry and stand it in the empty tin. Count how many came out the color she was expecting.
main.tip: Cold eggs take color better and crack less. Take them out of the fridge as you start.

outside.title: What the Neighbors Put Out
paras: Easter Sunday, and the street dresses up for it. Walk the block hunting for what people have put out: a wreath on a door, plastic eggs tied to a bush, daffodils in a pot on a step. She counts the doors with something on them and the doors without. Ask which one she would copy, and put that on your own door when you get in.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and everything he lifts goes to his mouth, so he stays clear of the tray and the vinegar. Wrap a hard-boiled egg in a clean burp cloth, knot it, and let him roll and squeeze that instead. Out on the block, lie him back in the stroller and let him watch the branches move over him.

second.title: The Egg Roll Race
second.intro: Eight dyed eggs come out of the tin, a plank goes on a book, and she chalks a line across the ground for the finish. They race two at a time and she makes the rules up as they go.
materials: 1 flattened cardboard box or a plank for the ramp
Chalk outdoors, or masking tape indoors
Your phone for the photo finish
steps: Prop one end of the plank on a book, a hand's height off the ground, so the first eggs survive.
She chalks a start line across the top and a finish line on the ground past the bottom.
Race two at a time, one in each hand. She counts down and you let go together.
Eggs do not roll straight. Chalk a mark where each one stops.
She will invent a rule around the fourth race: three goes each, no hands past the line, the blue one is out. Play by whatever she says.
Add the second book under the ramp and run the whole thing again. Ask her which egg goes furthest before she lets go of it.
Photograph the last two crossing the line, then the whole chalked ground from above.
second.tip: Cracks are part of it. An egg split down one side wobbles off in its own direction and becomes the favorite.

alternatives: Roll them down the stairs onto a cushion and skip the chalk.
Sort them into the egg carton by color and stop there.
Hide the dyed eggs and hunt them again with the basket.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, the Easter Sunday one, and take the basket
The duck pond, quieter than the park on a holiday
A drive to somewhere with a view and the rest of the chocolate
The playground on the way home if there is anything left in her
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 9 months and bangs one thing against another. Give him two wooden spoons at the bottom of the ramp and let him be the noise at the finish line. He will also pull himself up on the propped plank, so weight the books. Roll a soft ball down to him and watch him wait for the next one.

insight.headline: Chemical reactions she can see are the best first science.
paras: The fizz is carbon dioxide, made the instant the vinegar reaches the baking soda, and Azlyn has no need of the word. She needs the sequence: she did a thing, something different happened, and it happened every time. Cause and effect at three gets built out of repetitions like this one, with under a second between her action and the result. Slow reactions teach her less, because she cannot hold the two ends of a long wait together in her head. Keep the vinegar coming and let her run it eight times. The explanation can wait until she is five and asks for it.

days.safety: Vinegar stings eyes and she will rub hers with a wet hand. Keep a dry towel within her reach and wash her hands before she touches her face. The dyed eggs sat out all afternoon and rolled along the ground, so they are for looking at and never for eating. A whole egg and a shard of shell are both choking hazards for Kreston, and at 9 months he reaches anything left on a low table. Count the eggs back into the box.

days.title: Hiding and Waiting
days.prepTonight: Save six eggshell halves out of tonight's cooking, rinse them and stand them upside down to dry. Put the cress seed, a jam jar and one dried bean beside them.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Cress Cups on the Sill

opening.title: Twelve Little Parcels
opening.need: 12 small objects from round the house · newspaper or tissue · masking tape.
steps: Go round the house and pick twelve things worth finding: a hair clip, a sticker sheet, a wooden block, a teaspoon.
She wraps each one in a square of paper and tapes it. Loose and ugly is right, because they have to open fast.
Count them into her basket out loud. Twelve is the number for the whole day.

main.title: The Hunt She Hides
materials: 1 sheet of paper and a marker for the tally
1 dish towel to cover your eyes
steps: One room only. Say where the edges are and hold to them, because a hunt across the house runs an hour and ends in tears.
Sit down with the dish towel over your eyes and count to twenty out loud. She will narrate every hiding place. Pretend you heard none of it.
Hunt. Find three fast, then go slow and obvious. She talks you in with hot and cold.
Mark each one on the tally sheet as it comes in. Twelve found means twelve hidden, and she will want that count to come out.
Swap over. She hunts, you hide, and put two somewhere she has to move something to reach.
Third round, she hides again. The hiding places get better each time.
main.tip: Take far longer than you need. The pleasure for her is watching you walk past it twice.

outside.title: The Chalk Arrow Trail
paras: Chalk an arrow on the sidewalk outside the door, another twenty steps on, then keep going round the corner and along the wall. She follows them to something at the end: a stick you propped, the mailbox, a friend's gate. Let her chalk the trail home, in directions no one can read. The next rain takes the lot.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and object permanence is doing real work now. Hide a parcel under a cloth in front of him and let him pull it off. Run it six or seven times while Azlyn hides hers. Keep his parcel bigger than his fist and take the tape off, because tape ends up in his mouth.

second.title: Hair That Takes a Week
second.intro: Everything so far today has paid out inside a minute. Cress takes six days, and she checks it every morning until it comes up.
materials: 4–6 empty eggshell halves or paper cups
Cress or mustard seed (bird seed or dried lentils work)
1 sheet of paper and crayons for the chart
steps: Draw a face on each shell and stand them in the egg carton: hers, yours, Kreston's, Joseph's. The seed comes up out of the top as hair.
Tear paper towels into small pieces, ball them loose and pack each shell about two-thirds full.
She waters each one from the pitcher until the paper is soaked through with no puddle in the bottom. Soaked, not swimming.
A pinch of seed on top of each, pressed down with one finger. No soil and no covering. Cress grows on wet paper alone.

Line the jam jar with a folded strip of paper towels, wedge the bean between paper and glass at her eye height, and pour an inch of water in. She watches the root come out of the side, which a plant pot never lets her do.
Stand it all on the sill. Rule a chart with seven boxes, one for each morning, and she colors one box a day.
Photograph the sill today so there is something to hold Sunday's up against.
second.tip: Cress on a warm sill drinks fast. Give her the pitcher before breakfast and let her touch the paper to decide.

alternatives: One cup only, hers, and skip the faces.
Grow the bean in the jar and nothing else.
Draw what she thinks it will look like on Sunday and pin it above the sill.
outAgain: The big slide playground, and count the steps on the way up
The riverside path, to see the water high after a week of March rain
The woods loop, hunting the first wildflower leaves through the dead ones
A hunt outdoors, the twelve parcels again in somebody's yard
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 9 months and hauls himself up on anything with an edge, the windowsill included. Keep the shells at the back of the sill and lift him up to look. At the playground, sit him in the baby swing and push low and slow. He waves at the older children going past and some of them wave back.

insight.headline: Anticipation is a bigger pleasure than the payoff.
paras: The best hour of this week for Azlyn is the one before the hunt. Imaging work on reward finds the largest response arrives while a person waits for something good and drops off once the thing is in hand, and three-year-olds run on the same wiring. The waiting is where the pleasure sits. That is worth knowing on the afternoons you are tempted to hand over the treat to stop the asking. Stretch it instead: talk about the cress at breakfast, color in the chart, count the mornings left. She gets six good days out of one packet of seed.

days.safety: Cress seed, mustard seed and dried beans all fit a 9-month-old pincer grip and go straight to the mouth. Keep the packets shut and off the floor and sweep after she sows. Eggshell halves have edges sharp enough to cut a lip. Kreston pulls to stand on furniture this month, which puts the sill and the table edge in reach, and the jam jar comes down with him if he gets a hand to it.

days.title: Sink, Float, Spin
days.prepTonight: Boil four eggs and put them back in the box with two raw ones. Stand the salt, two tall jars and a deep tray by the sink, and put spare socks in the swimming bag.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Egg That Learns to Float

opening.title: Guessing Before the Water
opening.need: 8 small objects (a cork, a spoon, a stone, an orange, a plastic lid) · 2 empty bowls · a marker.
steps: Line the objects up on the table with two bowls behind them, one marked SINK and one FLOAT.
She sorts every object into a bowl with no water in sight. Take her guesses without comment and note the ones you think are wrong.
No testing yet. The bowls stay as she leaves them until the water arrives at 9:15.

main.title: The Egg That Learns to Float
materials: 1 scrap of paper, 1 marker and masking tape
The sink pile and float pile from the morning
steps: Test her two piles first. Fill the tray, and she drops each object in and moves it to the right bowl. Say so on the ones she called right.
Fill both jars two-thirds with warm water. Lower an egg into the first with the spoon. It sits on the bottom, which she predicted.
One tablespoon of salt at a time into the second jar, stirred until the water goes clear again. She counts the spoons.
Lower the second egg in around spoon five. Somewhere near eight it lifts off the bottom and rides at the top with a coin of shell showing.
Ask her what she thinks is holding it up. Write her answer word for word on a scrap and tape it to the glass.
Trickle plain water down the back of the spoon into the salty jar. The egg rises to the join and sits there, halfway up the glass, and she will make you look at it all week.
main.tip: Warm water takes salt fast and cold water sulks. If the egg will not lift, add two more spoons and stir for longer.

outside.title: Stick Races in the Gutter
paras: March rain leaves the gutters running for hours. Drop two sticks in at the top of the hill and walk down beside them, and the one she picked will lose. Find where the water speeds up and where it pools behind a drain grate. Poke the leaves clear and watch what changes. Rain boots on before you open the door.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and holds things between finger and thumb. Sit him at his own shallow tray on a towel: two inches of water, a plastic cup and a wooden spoon, both too big to swallow. He slaps the surface for the splash and hunts for it again. Never leave him alone beside it, not for the time it takes to answer the door.

second.title: Raw Egg, Cooked Egg
second.intro: Four eggs, two of them cooked, no way to tell from the outside. She works it out three ways without cracking one open.
steps: Mark the four eggs A, B, C and D. Tell her two are cooked and let her guess which before she touches anything.
Spin each one flat on the tray. The cooked ones go like a top. The raw ones wobble and stall, because the liquid inside keeps moving after the shell stops.
Spin one, stop it with a finger for half a second, then let go. A raw egg starts turning again on its own. A cooked one stays dead.
Hold each one against a flashlight or a bright window. The raw ones glow at the edges.
She sorts them into two groups and you write her decision on the tray before anyone checks.
Crack them into the bowl one at a time. Do the two she called cooked first.
Shells into the freezer bag, knot it, and everyone washes with soap before anything else.
second.tip: Say nothing about why the raw one wobbles until she has spun all four twice. She spots the pattern before she can explain it.

alternatives: Spinning only. Six cooked eggs and let her spin them until they crack.
Float an orange, then peel it and float it again.
Salt water in the bath for a bath toy that refuses to sink.
outAgain: Swimming, and try her on her back with your hand under her head
The indoor play center if the pool is shut for the holidays
The library, a day early
A warm café afterwards with her hair still wet
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool too. At 9 months he pulls to stand on the steps and the rail, so one hand stays on him the whole time on wet tiles. Twenty minutes is plenty. Hold him under the arms and walk him along the bottom. Dress him before yourself.

insight.headline: Prediction is the beginning of scientific thinking.
paras: Azlyn sorted a tray of objects into sink and float this morning before a drop of water came near them. Half her guesses were wrong, and the wrong ones earn their keep. A prediction turns a demonstration into her problem, and a child who has committed to an answer watches the test with an attention that a child being shown something never brings. The surprise of a guess that turns out wrong is what makes the answer stick, and she remembers the cork for having called it wrong. Take her guess at face value, write it down, and let it be wrong. She corrects the model herself.

days.safety: Raw egg goes on her hands, the tray and the counter. Wash with soap before anyone touches Kreston, the snack or a tap handle. Water on a hard floor is a fall hazard for a baby hauling himself upright on furniture. Mop as you go. At the pool, stay within arm's reach of both children the whole time.

days.title: Who Comes Out of an Egg
days.prepTonight: Find twenty animals in a magazine, a seed catalog or last year's calendar and leave the pile on the table with the scissors, two lengths of string, the scrap card and a marker.

opening.title: Twenty Animals on the Table
opening.need: the magazine pile · scissors · 2 lengths of string or 2 paper plates.
steps: She cuts out twenty animals, rough edges and all. Cut the awkward ones for her and keep her scissors moving.
Lay all twenty face up and name them together. Take her name for anything neither of you recognizes.
Set the two string circles on the floor side by side with the animals heaped between them. Say nothing yet about how they get sorted.

main.title: Hatched or Not Hatched
materials: 2 lengths of string, or 2 paper plates
2 pieces of scrap card for the words
1 animal book off the shelf to settle arguments
steps: Write HATCHED on one card and BORN on another and tape one to each circle. Give her both meanings once, in her language: came out of an egg, or came out of its mother.
Place two she knows for certain yourself, a chicken and a dog, one in each circle. Then hand her the heap.
She places every animal and says why. Repeat her reason back to her before you agree with it or check it.
The arguments will be the frog, the snake, the fish, the bat and the duck-billed platypus. Get the animal book down and look them up together instead of telling her.
Count each circle out loud once all twenty are down.
Move three animals across while she is out of the room, then send her back in to find the mistakes.
main.tip: Take the wrong answers at face value and ask what made her think so. A three-year-old who puts the bat in with the chickens has a reason.

outside.title: Grew or Made
paras: Walk the street sorting everything out loud into two piles: grew, or somebody made it. The bird grew, the trash can came out of a factory, and the pigeon standing on top of it gives her a moment's trouble. Ask about the fence, which somebody made out of something that grew. Bring one of each home.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and he sorts too, in his own system. He runs everything he lifts against three questions: does it make a noise, does it come apart, does it fit in my mouth. Give him the three biggest cut-outs, each one taped onto a piece of cereal card wider than his mouth. On the walk he waves at every dog, so stop and let one come to the stroller if the owner offers.

second.title: A Page for Every Animal
second.intro: The animals come out of the two circles this afternoon and turn into a book.
materials: The cut-outs out of both circles
steps: Fold one sheet in half, in half again, and once more. Open it out and cut along the folds for eight small pages. Same with the second sheet.
Stack them, fold the stack once down the middle and tape or staple the spine. She holds the fold while you do it.
One animal a page. She glues them down and you hold nothing straight for her. Crooked is correct.
Ask what she wants to say about each one and write it underneath in her words. Leave the grammar alone. He hatched out and he was all wet goes down as she said it.
Beside the hatchers she draws the egg. Beside the others she draws the mother.
The cover gets a title she picks and her name in marker, with the date small in the corner.
Read it back to her cover to cover, then put it in tonight's book pile.
second.tip: Read her words back with the mistakes in. Hearing her own sentence come out of a book is how she works out what writing is for.

alternatives: One page only, her favorite animal, done big.
Sort the cut-outs by number of legs instead.
Tape cut-outs to cereal card and make Kreston a board book.
Take the whole pile to the library and match them to photographs.
outAgain: The library, and ask at the desk for the nest and egg books
The indoor play center if the library is full of the holiday crowd
The park, and count the birds visible from one bench
A café with the new book, read twice
The pet store, to look at something that hatched
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him down in the board-book corner. At 9 months he pulls himself up on the low shelves, and he will empty one while Azlyn chooses hers. Let the emptying happen and put it back at the end. Pick him something with a flap.

insight.headline: Category words are a bigger deal than they look.
paras: Hatched and born are two words doing a great deal of work. Azlyn already sorts by color and by size, and today she sorted by something she cannot see. A category built on an invisible property lets her make a guess about an animal she has never met, from nothing except the group it sits in. A child who hears the group word alongside the object name (fruit, tool, bird, vehicle) has somewhere to file the next new one she meets. Use the group word out loud, and let her argue the edge cases. The arguing is her testing where the boundary runs.

days.safety: The string circles go back in the drawer as the sorting ends. String at toddler height is a strangulation risk, and a serious one, so it never stays on the floor while Kreston is down there. Scissors stay with you between cuts. Twenty paper cut-outs end up scattered and every one of them fits his pincer grip, so sweep before he goes down. His three taped cut-outs come back to you the moment you stop watching him.

days.title: Tricks and a Very Long Line
days.prepTonight: Set the breakfast table wrong once she is asleep: cups upside down, forks where the spoons go, her chair facing the wall, a shoe on her placemat, and the cereal box standing in the fridge. Leave the tape measure and masking tape by the front door.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Longest Line in the House

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks, in the Wrong Places

opening.title: Five Things Are Wrong
opening.need: the table you set wrong last night · 1 sheet of paper · a crayon.
steps: Sit down to breakfast as though nothing is out of place. Pour into the upside-down cup and keep a straight face.
She spots them one at a time. Draw a line on the paper for each and count them at the end.
Tell her it is April Fools' Day, that the day is built for tricks, and that at 9:15 she plans three for Joseph.

main.title: Three Tricks for Joseph
materials: A lump of playdough or scrunched paper for the pretend food
steps: Sit down with the paper and take her ideas first. Write them all down, then pick three that are harmless and she can do herself.
The plate: build his dinner out of playdough or scrunched paper, set it at his place and lay a dish towel over it.
The shoes: a ball of paper pushed into each toe so his foot stops an inch short. She counts them in, two shoes, two balls, so both come back out.
The mug: draw it, cut it out, tape it flat inside the cupboard where the real one lives, and hide the real one behind the cereal.
Rehearse the face. She has to say nothing until he walks in, so play Joseph at the door and make her hold it.
Write APRIL 1 on the back of the paper plate. She may want to do this every year.
main.tip: She will crack and tell him at the door. Count it a success anyway, because the hour she spent holding a secret was the hard part.

outside.title: The Walk Done Backwards
paras: Walk the usual route the wrong way round, from the far end. The lamppost she counts first comes last, the hill goes down instead of up, and the corner where she always runs arrives too soon. She will tell you it is wrong. Ask what comes next at every junction. Dandelions are up along the curbs and the hedges are green at the tips.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and has a sense of humor now. Put a bowl on your head and take it off, or offer him a toy and pull it back. Both get a laugh: he knows enough about how things ought to go to notice when they do not. Do the bowl six times and he pulls it off you himself.

second.title: The Longest Line in the House
second.intro: One line, starting at the front door, as long as she can make it. Everything she can carry is allowed in.
materials: Cans and boxes from the cupboard
Masking tape for the start line
1 tape measure or a length of string
1 laundry basket for putting it back
steps: Tape a start line across the floor at the front door and stand one shoe on it. Nothing goes in front of it.
One rule: she carries everything herself, one trip at a time. That holds the pace down.
Let the line find its own route: round the corner, under the table, up the stairs if it gets that far.
Once she runs out of toys, open the cupboard and hand over cans, boxes and packets. Nothing that opens, nothing from the fridge.
Measure it in her own feet, heel to toe, counting out loud. Measure it again with the tape and let her hear two different numbers for one line.
Photograph it from the front door before anything moves.
second.tip: Put the tidying inside the game. Sorting the line into two piles, her things and the kitchen's, goes faster than you expect.

alternatives: A line of one thing only: every shoe in the house.
Line up ten things and take one away while she is not looking.
Build a tower out of the cans instead and stop there.
outAgain: The garden center, and let her choose one packet of seed for the sill
The hardware store, to look at the long straight things
The park, for running after a morning of standing still
The duck pond with a handful of oats
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 9 months, and a floor covered in small objects is the best and worst thing to happen to him. Once her line is photographed and cleared, give him a short line of his own, four things too big to swallow, and let him knock it down. Keep him clear of the cans.

insight.headline: Lining things up is a developmental stage, not a red flag.
paras: Azlyn lines up her animals, her shoes and her crayons, and sooner or later somebody makes a face about it. Ordering objects in a row is standard three-year-old work and turns up in play everywhere anyone has looked. She is practicing one-to-one correspondence, seriation and spatial planning, all of which become counting and measuring inside a year. The lining up on its own says nothing worrying. The thing worth watching is whether she can be interrupted, and a child who laughs at a daft item you add is doing what she should. If she cannot be interrupted, that is not a diagnosis. Plenty of three-year-olds guard a line fiercely. If it sits with you, mention it at her next check-up.

days.safety: The floor is covered end to end in small objects, and Kreston pulls up on everything, cruises into furniture and mouths what he lifts. Keep him in the carrier, the high chair or behind a gate while the line is down, and clear it before he goes back on the floor. No trick gets played on Kreston, and nothing hides Azlyn's food or her comfort toy.
